title: Cloud Computing Fundamentals
description: Service models, shared responsibility, compute, storage, networking, scaling, resilience, and cloud costs.

questions.prompt: Your team moves a self-managed PostgreSQL server from an EC2 VM to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which task does your team still own?

options.text: Patching the operating system of the database host
Replacing failed storage hardware under the database
Creating database users and granting them least-privilege permissions
Physically securing the data center that hosts it

questions.explanation: With a managed service, AWS operates the host OS, hardware, and facilities, but customers always own their data and who can access it, including database accounts and grants. OS patching moves from you to AWS when you leave EC2 for RDS.

questions.prompt: A three-person team has a Python web app. They want to deploy their code and have the platform handle OS patching, runtime updates, and load balancing, while they keep full control of the application code. Which service model fits?

options.text: IaaS, e.g., Amazon EC2 virtual machines
PaaS, e.g., Azure App Service or Google App Engine
SaaS, e.g., Salesforce or Microsoft 365
On-premises virtualization, e.g., VMware vSphere

questions.explanation: PaaS runs your code on a managed runtime, so the provider handles the OS, runtime, and scaling plumbing. IaaS would leave OS patching and load-balancer setup to the team, and SaaS provides finished software rather than hosting their code.

questions.prompt: An online store runs on two identical, stateless web servers behind a load balancer. Traffic triples on Black Friday for about 12 hours. What is the most cost-effective cloud approach?

options.text: Use an autoscaling group that adds instances as load rises and removes them afterward
Permanently resize both servers to instance types three times larger
Buy 3-year reservations for enough servers to cover the peak year-round
Move the database to a bigger instance and leave the web tier unchanged

questions.explanation: Stateless servers behind a load balancer can scale horizontally, and elasticity means paying for the extra capacity only during the 12-hour peak. Permanently sizing or reserving for the peak pays for idle capacity the rest of the year.

questions.prompt: An internal tool's HTTP endpoint is called about 200 times a day, and each request takes about 300 ms. It runs on a VM that is up 24/7 and idle more than 99% of the time. Which option most reduces cost while keeping it available on demand?

options.text: Move the VM to a larger instance type covered by a 3-year reservation
Add a second VM in another availability zone for redundancy
Keep the VM and enable autoscaling with a minimum of one instance
Move it to a serverless function (e.g., AWS Lambda), billed per request and run time

questions.explanation: Serverless functions bill per invocation and execution time, with no charge while idle, and here that's only about one minute of compute per day. Autoscaling with a minimum of one instance still pays for an always-on VM.

questions.prompt: True or false: running VMs in three Availability Zones of a single region protects the application from an outage of that entire region.
questions.explanation: Availability Zones are isolated data centers within one region, so spreading across them protects against a data-center-level failure. Surviving a regional outage requires deploying to a second region.

questions.prompt: Four Linux VMs running a legacy content-management app must read and write the same directory tree at the same time, through ordinary POSIX file paths. Which AWS storage option fits?

options.text: A single Amazon EBS gp3 volume attached to all four VMs
An Amazon S3 bucket the app reads and writes through its API
An Amazon EFS file system mounted on all four VMs
Local instance store volumes, one on each of the four VMs

questions.explanation: EFS is a managed NFS file system built for concurrent shared access from many instances. A gp3 EBS volume attaches to only one instance at a time, and S3 is object storage accessed through an API, not POSIX paths.

questions.prompt: Using the pricing below, which purchase option is cheaper for this one instance, and by how much per month?

code.source:
Instance: 1 x general-purpose VM
On-demand:                 $0.20/hour, billed only while running
1-year reserved, no upfront: $0.12/hour, billed for every hour of the term
Workload: runs 10 hours/day, every day
Assume a 30-day month (720 hours)

options.text: Reserved; it saves $24.00 per month
Reserved; it saves $57.60 per month
On-demand; it is $26.40 per month cheaper
Neither; both cost $60.00 per month

questions.explanation: On-demand: 300 h x $0.20 = $60.00. Reserved bills every hour of the term: 720 h x $0.12 = $86.40, so on-demand is $26.40 cheaper. The $24.00 answer wrongly applies the reserved rate only to hours used; reservations pay off only for steady, high-utilization workloads.

questions.prompt: Instances in this private subnet (no public IPs) must download OS patches from the internet but must not be reachable from it. Given the route table below, what should you add?

code.source:
Route table: rtb-private  (associated with subnet-app-a)
Destination      Target
10.0.0.0/16      local

options.text: A 0.0.0.0/0 route to the VPC's internet gateway
A 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT gateway placed in a public subnet
A 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT gateway placed in this same private subnet
An inbound security group rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443

questions.explanation: A NAT gateway in a public subnet (which routes to the internet gateway) lets private instances start outbound connections while blocking unsolicited inbound ones. A NAT gateway inside the private subnet has no path to the internet gateway, and instances without public IPs can't use an internet gateway route directly.

questions.prompt: The web servers' security group allows inbound TCP 443, but clients' HTTPS connections time out. The subnet's network ACL is shown below. What is the cause?

code.source:
Network ACL for subnet-web (public)
Inbound
  Rule 100  TCP  port 443   0.0.0.0/0  ALLOW
  Rule *    ALL  ALL        0.0.0.0/0  DENY
Outbound
  Rule 100  TCP  port 443   0.0.0.0/0  ALLOW
  Rule *    ALL  ALL        0.0.0.0/0  DENY

options.text: NACLs are stateless; replies go to clients' ephemeral ports, which the outbound rules block
Security groups are stateless, so they also need an outbound rule for port 443
The `*` rule is evaluated first, so it denies all traffic before rule 100
Inbound rule 100 must match source port 443 instead of destination port 443

questions.explanation: Network ACLs don't track connections, so response traffic must be allowed explicitly: outbound TCP to ports 1024-65535 here. Security groups are the stateful layer, and NACL rules are evaluated in ascending number order with `*` last.

questions.prompt: Your company runs its application on Amazon EC2 instances. Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which of these are your company's responsibility? Select all that apply.

options.text: Applying security patches to the guest operating system
Patching the hypervisor that runs the instances
Configuring security group rules
Physical security of the data center
Enabling encryption for sensitive data on EBS volumes and controlling key access
Replacing failed disks in the physical host

questions.explanation: With IaaS the customer manages everything from the guest OS up, including network firewall configuration and data protection choices. AWS is responsible for security 'of' the cloud: the facilities, hardware, and virtualization layer.

questions.prompt: A user whose only permissions come from this policy runs `aws s3 cp s3://reports-bucket/q3.csv .` successfully, but `aws s3 ls s3://reports-bucket` returns AccessDenied. Why?

options.text: The `/*` wildcard matches only one level, so listing nested prefixes is denied
Version 2012-10-17 is a legacy policy version that cannot allow list actions
`aws s3 ls` always requires `s3:ListAllMyBuckets` on every resource
Listing needs `s3:ListBucket` on the bucket ARN itself, which the policy never grants

questions.explanation: Object actions like GetObject apply to `bucket/*`, but listing is a bucket-level action (s3:ListBucket) on `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket`. IAM's `*` matches across `/` characters, and ListAllMyBuckets is needed only for `aws s3 ls` with no bucket named.

questions.prompt: Workers in private subnets download about 40 TB a month from Amazon S3 buckets in the same region through a NAT gateway, and NAT gateway data processing is now the largest line on the AWS bill. Which change removes that charge with the least effort?

options.text: Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint to the private subnets' route tables
Add a second NAT gateway in another AZ to split the traffic
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the source buckets
Turn on S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the objects being read

questions.explanation: A gateway endpoint routes S3 traffic privately through route-table entries and carries no hourly or per-GB charge, so the traffic stops passing through the NAT gateway. More NAT gateways still bill per GB processed, and Transfer Acceleration adds cost for long-distance uploads.

questions.prompt: Using AWS's four disaster recovery strategies, which one meets the approved requirements below?

code.source:
Order database - DR requirements (approved by the business)
RPO:        <= 1 minute
RTO:        <= 1 hour
Constraint: lowest ongoing cost that meets both targets

Measured cross-region DB replication lag:  < 5 s
Tested app-tier rebuild from IaC:          ~25 min

options.text: Backup and restore: nightly snapshots copied to a second region
Pilot light: continuous replication to a second region, app tier provisioned via IaC on failover
Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully running copy of the stack in a second region
Multi-site active/active: full capacity serving traffic in both regions

questions.explanation: With replication lag under 5 seconds and a tested 25-minute app-tier rebuild, pilot light meets both targets while running only the replicated database day to day. Nightly snapshots risk up to 24 hours of data loss, and warm standby or active/active also meet the targets but cost more to keep running.

questions.prompt: A worker fleet scales on average CPU above 70%. Each worker processes queue messages by calling a slow external API. Metrics are below. What change fixes the scaling behavior?

code.source:
Time   Instances  Avg CPU  Queue depth  Oldest msg age
09:00  4          22%       1,200        40 s
10:00  4          25%      18,500        14 min
11:00  4          24%      61,000        52 min

options.text: Lower the CPU scaling threshold from 70% to 50% so it reacts sooner
Switch to larger instance types with more vCPUs per worker
Increase the queue's visibility timeout so messages wait longer
Scale on queue backlog per instance (or oldest-message age) instead of CPU

questions.explanation: The workers are I/O-bound, waiting on the API, so CPU stays low while the backlog explodes; the metric doesn't reflect the actual bottleneck. AWS recommends scaling SQS consumers on backlog per instance, while a 50% CPU threshold would still never trigger at 25% CPU.

questions.prompt: A nightly 6-hour rendering job runs on one large Spot Instance. About twice a month it is interrupted late in the run and restarts from zero, missing the morning deadline. Which change keeps Spot's savings while reliably meeting the deadline?

options.text: Set a much higher maximum Spot price so AWS never reclaims the instance
Pin the request to one instance type in one AZ for consistent capacity
Split the job into checkpointed chunks spread across several instance types and AZs
Use a larger Spot instance so the job finishes before any interruption

questions.explanation: Spot capacity can be reclaimed at any time with a two-minute notice, so the fix is limiting lost work (checkpoints) and drawing from multiple capacity pools. Interruptions are driven mainly by capacity, so a higher max price doesn't prevent them, and a single pool raises the risk.
